client: I've been feeling really heavy ever since my grandmother passed away last month. It's like everything I used to enjoy just feels flat now — I'll try to watch a show or go for a walk and there's just nothing there, no pleasure in any of it. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because she's still gone no matter what I say here.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds truly exhausting — a deep, quiet grief that's taken the color out of things you used to love, and I can hear in the softness of your voice just how heavy that weight feels. You're right that talking won't bring her back, and I want to honor that truth rather than dismiss it. But what we can do together is make a little more room for you to carry this grief without it swallowing everything — not to fix the loss, but so you don't have to feel quite so alone inside it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that's a slightly different way of putting it — not fixing it, just making room for it. I don't fully know what that even means in practice, though, because right now it feels like the grief is just everywhere, all the time, and I don't see how talking creates any kind of space when I already think about her constantly. But I'm here, so I suppose some part of me is willing to try, even if I'm not sure it'll do anything.
therapist: That part of you that showed up today, even uncertain, even doubtful — that matters, and I don't want to gloss over it. Your voice carries something that sounds like a quiet exhaustion, like you've been holding this so carefully for so long that even the idea of putting it down somewhere feels abstract. "Making room" might just mean that instead of grief ambushing you constantly, we slowly help you find moments where *you* choose to turn toward it — which is different from it swallowing you whole without warning.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That distinction you're making — choosing to turn toward it versus being ambushed by it — I can intellectually understand the difference, but I honestly don't know how I'd even do that. Like, what does choosing to grieve actually look like? Because right now it just happens to me, it hits me when I'm in the middle of making coffee or something, and I can't imagine intentionally inviting that feeling in.
therapist: There's something in your voice — a kind of tense, searching quality — that tells me this isn't just an intellectual puzzle for you, it's a real and urgent question. Choosing to grieve can look surprisingly small at first — maybe setting aside ten minutes to look at a photo of her, or writing down one memory, so that grief has a *container* rather than leaking into every cup of coffee uninvited. The goal isn't to feel it more intensely, but to give it a designated place so the rest of your day doesn't have to be constantly braced for impact.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: The idea of looking at a photo actually makes my stomach tighten just thinking about it, like I'm not sure I'm ready to do that on purpose rather than accidentally stumbling across one. I can see the logic in what you're describing, giving grief a container, but I'm worried that if I open that door intentionally I won't be able to close it again and I'll just fall apart completely. I have things I have to do, I can't just be a mess for the rest of the day after a ten-minute grief session.
therapist: The way you just spoke — quick, pitched high, like your thoughts were racing ahead of themselves — tells me that fear of falling apart is very real and very present for you right now, not just a hypothetical worry. That belief, *"if I open this door I won't be able to close it,"* is worth gently examining, because most people find that grief, when approached in small and boundaried ways, doesn't actually swallow them whole — it tends to peak and then subside, like a wave rather than a flood. So before we try anything, what if we just noticed that fear together, without doing anything yet — because respecting your own readiness is actually part of the process, not an obstacle to it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I appreciate that you're not pushing me to do the photo thing right now, that actually makes me breathe a little easier. But I'm also noticing that even just sitting here talking about the fear of falling apart is making my chest feel tight, which I guess is kind of ironic — I'm already feeling it just from describing my worry about feeling it. I don't know if that means I'm more ready than I think, or just that grief is already so close to the surface that there's really no avoiding it anyway.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, pitched high, like your body is running just slightly ahead of your words — actually mirrors exactly what you're describing, that grief is already right there at the surface, not waiting behind some door you have to unlock. And I think your own observation is really insightful: the fact that you're feeling it *right now*, in this conversation, and you haven't fallen apart, is quiet evidence against the belief that opening the door means losing control completely. You're already doing the thing you were afraid of, just by being here and saying it out loud.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's... actually a little hard to argue with, and I wasn't expecting that. I'm still here, my chest is tight, my eyes are getting a little watery, and I haven't completely fallen apart — which I guess is something, even if it doesn't feel triumphant or anything. I think part of me still worries that this conversation has a clear ending time and I can pull myself together before I leave, but what about when I'm alone at home tonight and there's no structure around it?
therapist: The quietness in your voice right now, soft and a little fragile, tells me this moment is genuinely tender — and what you just noticed about yourself is real progress, even if it doesn't feel like a victory. For tonight, what if the structure doesn't have to disappear entirely — maybe you give yourself permission to feel it for a set time, even just saying out loud "I'm going to sit with this for a few minutes," so it's still *you* choosing, rather than being ambushed alone in the dark. You've already shown yourself today that the wave can come and you can still be standing — that's something you can take home with you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe I can do that tonight, just saying out loud that I'm choosing to sit with it for a few minutes, but I'm also a little worried it'll feel silly or forced when I'm alone in my apartment with no one there to witness it or hold me accountable. And there's this other thing I haven't said yet — part of why being alone with the grief feels so hard is that my grandmother was actually one of the people I would have called when I was struggling, and now that specific comfort is exactly what I've lost. So it's not just grief, it's also that the person I'd normally lean on is the one who's gone.
therapist: What you just shared — spoken so quickly and softly, like it's been pressing against you waiting to come out — feels like the heart of everything, that the grief is doubled because she wasn't just someone you lost, she was your way of surviving loss. That's not a small thing, and it reframes so much of why being alone with this feels so unbearable. And it makes complete sense that saying something out loud in an empty apartment feels hollow, because the voice you most want to hear answer back is the one that's gone — so part of what we might gently work toward is finding what it meant to be comforted by her, and how you might begin to offer some of that to yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: When you put it that way, that she was my way of surviving loss, something in me just kind of cracked open a little, because that's exactly it and I hadn't found those words for it myself. But the idea of offering that comfort to myself feels almost impossible, like I wouldn't even know where to start — she had this specific way of just listening without trying to fix anything, and I don't know how you replicate that from the inside. It also feels a little lonely to even try, like I'd just be reminded all over again that I'm doing it alone.
therapist: Your voice is soft and quick, like something delicate just shifted inside you, and I want to sit with that for a moment rather than rush past it. What you're describing — her gift of listening without fixing — is something you actually know intimately, because you received it so many times, and in a quiet way you're already doing it right now by letting yourself be heard without demanding answers from yourself. The loneliness of doing it alone is real and I won't minimize that, but you carry her way of listening inside you more than you might realize, because we learn how to be with ourselves from the people who were truly with us.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That idea that I carry her way of listening inside me — I want it to be true, and something about it feels almost true, but it also feels like something I might only be able to believe on a good day and not when I'm really struggling at midnight and the apartment is quiet. I guess I'm also noticing a little guilt creeping in, like if I can learn to comfort myself then somehow that means I need her less, and that feels like a kind of betrayal even though I know rationally it probably isn't. Does that make any sense, or am I just making this more complicated than it needs to be?
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, high, like the words are tumbling out under pressure — tells me this guilt caught you a little off guard, and I want you to know it makes complete sense, because love often disguises itself as loyalty to pain. But here's a gentle reframe: learning to comfort yourself isn't needing her less, it's actually carrying her *forward* — the comfort she gave you doesn't disappear when you internalize it, it becomes a living part of how she still exists in you. That's not betrayal; that might actually be one of the most profound ways we keep loving someone after they're gone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That framing — carrying her forward rather than needing her less — actually lands somewhere different than I expected, and I can feel my chest loosening just a tiny bit around it, like it's creating a small amount of breathing room where there wasn't any before. But I'm also aware that I might hear those words right now and feel them, and then tonight or tomorrow the guilt will come back and they won't stick the same way. How do I hold onto something like that when grief has a way of just washing over everything and making it hard to remember what felt true in a calmer moment?
therapist: Your voice is soft and a little breathless right now, like something just gently opened, and I want to honor that small loosening in your chest as real — even if it feels fragile. One thing that can help is writing that phrase down tonight, not to force the feeling back, but so that when the grief washes over and your mind goes flat, you have something in your own handwriting to find — a note from the calmer version of you to the midnight version. You don't have to hold onto the feeling; you just have to leave yourself a trail back to it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
